AN INTERVIEW WITH
JIMMY MCPARTLAND
FOR THE
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTE
DPA INTERVIEW
(TAPE TWO) (Tape 1)

And we are in my apartment in the Hotel Chelsea which is rather famous for people like Jimmy McPartland although he doesn't live here. And historically it has had most of the greatest artists in all fields either spending some time here or living here over a period of years.

Now this period, this interview rather, is part of oral history project funded by the National Endowment For The Arts in Washington which is a Federal Farm and it has conducted, this interview has been conducted for it as part of the Jazz Interaction connection collection with the National Endowment. In other words, Jazz Interactions is implementing this program for the National Endowment.

Altogether there are eight jazz musicians being interviewed. And I think that I'm one of the luckiest of the interviewers to have Jimmy McPartland. Lois McClous is the Project Coordinator and she is assisted by Pastor John Gensel who is known, well known
in New York as the pastor to the jazz community.

And I think perhaps one of the nicest ways of setting the tone for what follows is to listen to Jimmy McPartland on record for a few minutes. And I think we should start with the number which he first played back about 1930 which is called 'Singing the Blues'. And of course we know the blues structure and there is a long line and the long line in this one is until my daddy comes home. (LAUGHTER).
The very clear cornet that you're going to hear is that of Jimmy McPartland.
(MUSICAL RECORDING)

In a day when it's very, very popular to talk about highs, different kinds of highs, I'm going to have to say that that was a real high. And the only way to go from there is further up. (LAUGHTER). Now Jimmy you want to talk perhaps a little bit about the other fellows who were on that recording with you?

Oh, the clarinetist was, Peanuts Hucko the clarinet player I should say is Peter (Taco?). And the trombone player is Lou McGarity. And George Wettling is on drums and on down the line, so on and so forth. Do you want to go through all that?
Now was that your own band?
That was my own band.
That was your own band.
My own band yes. And it was made around 1956 I think it was. It was more or less a tribute to Bix Beiderbecke. Those are numbers that he did. And that was one of them.
Well since you mentioned that, name (LAUGHTER) we just have to go right on to Bix right here because certainly when we talk of writers we always think in terms, in terms of their influences.
That's right.

And certainly Bix Beiderbecke and Louis Armstrong of course were great influences in your life. I don't need to ask you anything here because I'm just going to sit back now and let you talk about Bix and Louis and Chicago and, what was it that highschool group?
Austin High Gang.
The Austin High Gang.
(LAUGHTER).
The Austin Highschool Gang, yes. And there's a reason for calling us a gang too.
Well go ahead.

Well I haven't mentioned it to you yet, but my father was a professional boxer, a professional musician and a professional baseball player. So he taught my brother and I since we were kids, since we were five years old we both started to learn how to play the violin. And also to learn to box, and to play baseball.

So we got to be good athletes you know. Good boxers, we could handle ourselves in any street fights or gangs like we used to have in those days on the west side of Chicago. And we could box and we could hit pretty hard. So what happened was, we started to play together with a jazz band. We didn't have a name for the band. And me being the cornet player, I was the leader. And I was almost like the leader of the gang because in crowds when any trouble would start why my brother would say, okay Cocky, you want to go? You know, ....
I take it that was your family nickname?
Well, my brother used to call me Cocky because I was cocky in those days. I was just a young kid you know and I thought I could hit pretty

hard and I used to win a lot of fights. So what happened with the Austin Highschool Gang, the reason they called us a gang was we'd get around to playing some of these fraternities. We played many places, at the drop of a hat that would just invite us. We played any place. We played on the street, any place. Sometimes the kids wouldn't even drop a hat (LAUGHTER). Any place at all. We just loved to play. It was our life.

But we played a few of these fraternities meetings and so on and so forth. And at one of them some man guy said, that stinks! It's awful you guys, what are you playing? You know, it stinks! And I said, stinks? And turned around to my brother and I said, come here, come here and tell me that. Come out and tell my brother come here, you know, what did you say? He said, it stinks! And my brother gave me the wink and man I started swinging. (LAUGHTER).

Yes, I started fighting, that's it. After that had happened a couple of times the rest of the guys around there said, if you don't like their music don't tell them about it, because that's a gang. (LAUGHTER). They will knock you around so don't mention that you don't like it. So they said, well the Austin Highschool Gang. We were like a gang. And that's it.
Do you think that fellow's objection was to the kind of music that you were playing because Chicago was filled with Europeans who still liked European waltzes and jantes and all kinds of....

That's right. That was the popular music of the day you know. Things that they could understand much better. They didn't understand our improvising and playing jazz. But they shouldn't have, you know say, don't say those words, you know, that's not nice. Don't insult us. So they finally got the idea you know, they didn't say those things any more.
The word got around, watch out for that Austin Highschool Gang because, you know. That was it. You want to know about Bix?

Yes. And I think that since you mentioned the Austin Highschool Gang though, that we might say right here that later on most of the men, or the boys I guess you might call them at the time that they played, that you played together, later became part of your very important band. And most of them became outstanding musicians beyond that.

Well you know what might be a good idea to explain how we got started. Wanting to play jazz music. And we were all going together a bunch of us guys at the Austin Highschool. Most of us played violins. Frank (Teschmacher) did, my brother, became my brother inlaw, Jim (Slanigan), my brother played violin.
What was your brother's name?

Richard. And we used to be together, We used to go to a place called 'The Spoon and Straw'. We'd go after highschool (COUGHS), excuse me. Go after highschool and have a malted milk and a sandwich, you know what the kids do. So we used to have a phonograph machine, and it was a lamp actually. The machine was a lamp and all the records were laying on the table there and they were 78s in those days. This is 1922.
And we'd pick up the records and play them. And put them on the machine and have our malted milk and sandwich and see the new records.
So there were some new ones in one day. There were some new records came in and that was the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. And then there was King Oliver

and man we put those on and we listened to those records. King Oliver and Louis Armstrong were blowing and the New Orleans Rhythm Kings and we just flipped our heads. And we said, man this is it, jazz, you know.
So, we all decided right then and there to get instruments and form our own band, right? And that's what we did. And I played the coronet you know.
Did you teach yourself how to play?

No, no, no. My father was a professional musician and he was a teacher. Also as I mentioned before, he had been a professional boxer and a professional base ball player, but now he was a music teacher. So we, my brother and I, we had played violin since we were five years old. And he taught us how to read and play the violin which was good for our intonation, our ears, to play in tune and other things.

I wasn't that interested in playing an instrument until we heard this jazz you know. None of us were really, see. Because we had all played classical things and operas and stuff like that. And when we heard this jazz we flipped. That was it.

We got instruments. And we went to my dad and said, we want to learn, I want to learn to play the cornet. Bud Freeman wanted to play the saxophone, Teschemacher the clarinet and my brother guitar and my brother-inlaw bass. And then a little later on we got Davie Tough (Bull) on drums from Park Highschool. And another guy by the name of Dave North on piano, so that was our band.
And we just practiced and studied and after we all got, it only took us a couple of weeks really to start playing the horns.
Oh really?
Yes. We just got, we played ....
Because you knew music, you knew how to read, you had ground work already.

That's right. That's right. So, we just studied. My dad, about two or three weeks we had on these instruments. Then we got out the took phonograph machine and just put the things right off the records two bars at a time. Number that were Louis Armstrong and King Oliver played and New Orleans Rhythm Kings. And we just got, we started playing these songs. You know we practiced every day after

school. As soon as we finished, go home and have dinner. Come back again after dinner at somebody's house in one of our houses and then play all night long until eleven, until ten or eleven o'clock at night. And inside of, I guess we got our first tune down, which was I think, 'Farewell Blues' something like that. I think it was. We had that down in about two weeks.

And then we improved our repertoire and got a next number, we'd get the next number and inside of two or three months we had a repertoire of four or five numbers, that we could play. And the blues we would get from the King Oliver records you know and Louis Armstrong. And then we found out that King Oliver was playing out on the South Side in Chicago there at the Lincoln Gardens. And we heard that Louis Armstrong was with him and we used to go out there. We were sixteen years old then you know. I was sixteen I mean. And we'd go out and hear them out there and we were just in seventh heaven.
We were so inspired that that's all we did. We just played music every day, every day and every night. Every day and every night. And naturally my
greatest influence on the cornet was first Paul Mares with the New Orleans Rhythm Kings.
Now was that a negro band?
No, it was a white group.
But then there was King Oliver and Louis Armstrong.
who were negro of course.
(LAUGHTER).

Oh yes. And that was the influence. And then, at first. And we used to copy their numbers off the records. But we never would copy their solos. You had to play your own solo. We made that one of our rules that we all had, in other words we could play the ensemble the way Louis or King played them or Paul Mares. But then we had to play your own solos. You had to do your own individual solo the way you feel.

And we, that's the way we did until we heard the next record that came out a few months later, it was the Wolverines. And the cornet player was Bix Beiderbecke. Well he had such beautiful tone you know, that man I said that tone is lovely, that's the tone for me. And so my influences actually came out of King Oliver of Louis Armstrong, Paul Mares and Bix Beiderbecke.
Mares Mares
Now is that Mares for Mares?

Yes. Well that was just a start off. I mean a start off because influences, I mean these are all good these guys. I mean King Oliver, Louis Armstrong and Paul Mares and then Bix Beiderbecke. And of course in playing jazz music you'll always hear some cornet player or someone, always something comes into Louis. You can't help it because it's subconsciously in your mind.

You don't mean to copy him but it just comes out there because you're playing what's in your mind and that subconscious comes out Louis in jazz. You never know it actually when you play, when you're playing. It's all improvised.

There's one good thing about tapes now and that is that you can catch yourself doing this kind of thing better than you could before when you had no way unless you were making a record. Of hearing what you had actually done. Do you know what I mean?
No, I don't understand you.
In other words, if you were to play something before the days of tape recorders....
Oh yes.
It, it was gone.
It was gone, sure.
It was gone. And you didn't have the advantage of being able to play it back to study what you had just done.

That's true. That's right. That's a great lesson that you learn when you first start recording. I mean that we learned rather years ago when we first started recording. What a great lesson in how to improve yourself and what NOT to do you know.
And these subconscious things that you were talking about, you had no way of really detecting the extent to which they had crept into your .....
Oh the improvisation?
You couldn't hear, yes.

Oh you'd never know because once you play something you just never know. I mean I've listened to records of mine. Some of them I can't stand, they're horrible. But I mean to me, but other people like them. But to me I don't like them at all.
What was your father's attitude towards jazz?
Oh he liked it. He was more, he was in ragtime field which is, to us was sort of corny like. We used to call it corny.
Oh really?

Yes. Because, I don't know, it has to flow, it had to flow you know and it was a little too jerky for us in those days. We liked King Oliver and Louis Armstrong and the Wolverines. We started, Bix Beiderbecke and those guys.
In other words you moved almost immediately from classical into jazz. (While going through ragtime?). (LAUGHTER).

Yes, but I haven't told you something to actually go way back before this. I'd like to mention this. That my first influence that I recognized, the two, my brother and I did. You see I was born on Lake and Polina Street on the West Side of Chicago and it was a mixed neighborhood. We had everyone. The whole, all kinds. Polish, Italian, Irish, Negro or blacks whichever you call them.
No, we were negroes then.
(LAUGHTER).

That's right, or colored people. Colored people. Because I know my mother, heard, heard one of my mother she was not one of us, was what our friends talk about a nigger you know. And my mother told us right then and there, don't you ever let me hear you say that word again. Call a black person a nigger. They are colored people.

And that's what they are is colored people. You're a white person and you are Irish and you wouldn't want someone to call you a shanty Irishman would you? Those are fighting words. No, we wouldn't mama.
Now we were about ten years old. I was ten years old then.
You were lace curtain Irish.
(LAUGHTER).
That's right. Well my mother came from Scotland. But my father came from Burlington, Iowa but his family came..... But it was an insult to call somebody an Shanty Irishman.
Of course it was, yes.

And I remembered my mother explained to us the same thing when you call a person a nigger, that is not it. You are insulting them period. You call them a colored person, they are a colored person. That's the way you refer to a colored

person.
And she had it then, she was right you know.
But we did, that's the way it was.
But you were talking about the influences though in this particular mixed neighborhood.

Ah, here's what happened. Now my brother and I had always played violin and I had played a little bit of the peck horn, and he played E-flat alto horn, in my father's band at picnics and things. It was a regular band you know, marching band style, that kind of stuff. And so forth.

And so I had musical training already. Now one night, it was a mixed neighborhood as I say, on Lake and Polina Lincoln Street on the West Side of Chicago. And there were eight colored men, blind colored men who heard this music across the street. Two or three basses and banjos and a guitar, mandolin and guitar. And they were singing spirituals. Gospel music. And my brother and I were, let me preface this by saying this. We were tough little monkeys in those days. Rough kids, you know, that's a tough neighborhood. And we would steal everything we could lay our hands on. We were bad.

Had a gang and everything else. Hermitage Gang.
So we could hear this music and go over to see these

eight guys and blind, all blind and playing this music which was really something. They were playing spirituals and it's swinging. It's rocking, it's going. And my God, my brother and I just flipped man. They're singing and the band is, you know, these spirituals.

And my brother and I started passing the hat for them and the people started putting the money in the hat for them and everything like that, and we gave them every penny. You can imagine, that was a compliment to them. (LAUGHTER). They must have been good because we loved them and we didn't even steal one penny from them.

We passed the hat for them. We got all this money and kept giving it to the guys there you know. And they were thanking us. But we'd listen, and they used to come a couple of times a week and play. But they were really the spirituals. I don't mean ....... ............(IMITATES SOUND OF SPIRITUALS).... ...
Oh, (you've got a good bass in there haven't you?)?
(CONTINUES TO IMITATE SOUND OF SPIRITUALS)................................
Well man, it was swinging and that's where we really got our first feeling for we could call it jazz. But gospel music, spiritual music, that was it.

And then we recognised it in the jazz. So that is really our first influence and it should be recognised. And as I think you and I talked before we turned the tape on that we both quite agree, I mean to me African rhythms and the rhythms and the sound of the drums and everything like that is your basic jazz beat. To me it's a religion within itself, the beat. It's a feeling that you get inside.
And then with the European harmonies and melodic lines and put that in and make the wedding, make the wedding and now you have American jazz. American music.

American music. The...only one, because every European group brought its own music with it. It's own rhythm. And none of that music became established of course, as you well know, as the American music.
Right, this is America.
It was this blend.
The wedding of the races.
The African rhythem and the
European melody. That's the American music.
That's correct. That's how I've always felt about it too. The melodic line and the harmonies of the Europeans and the African rhythm which is the real.....
Of course that's the Afro-American contribution. the American Constitution.
True, true, true, true. Well that's American jazz.
Oh, of course. Yes. Well listen, you were mentioning Beiderbecke before you started out with these other influences. And I know you want to talk about him because he was the biggest thing.......

Well it's just a matter of taste there I would say. A matter of an individual's taste in which direction he goes and what his influences are. I mean how can you, King Oliver, Louis Armstrong, I mean the great est these guys, Oh my goodness you know.
But the question is is their influence upon Bix Beiderbecke?
Oh of course, of course. Of course. You are always influenced by someone else.

However, then you go off in your own direction and you become yourself, musically that is. Your own personality, how you feel. But I did like, of course the way King Oliver and Louis Armstrong were swinging. I mean the way they were swinging......
Can you imitate King Oliver now?
On the horn?
Yes.

Well not really. The one thing I remember that he did, he and Louis did together, because Louis was his second cornet player then. At the Lincoln Gardens, that's when we used to go and listen to them there. And they loved us and of course we loved them you know. And Louis and King would come and sit down with us kids you know. My boys, Louis used to say, my boys.

But the thing that King and Louis did was 'Snake Rag' that was the name of the number that they played. They did two cornets duet, one of the breaks there was, it was King's break I know, King Oliver group. (IMITATES SOUND).................... (LAUGHTER). Yes, that was great, but I mean I just

remembered that. But to me it's hard to imitate another guy. But it does come into your playing every now and then. Subconsciously you just, you know you don't know and it just sneaks in there. Because it's way back in the recesses of your mind. In my mind because when I play I just have no idea in which direction I'm going. I know what the meddy is and harmony and I can hear all that. These things pop up now and then which is a compliment to you know the good taste that your mind, I think, my mind retains. Puts it way back there in the recesses some place and then eventually it will pop out and you'll say, where did that come from? You know?
Yes, yes.

But Bix was, I liked the musical sound of his tone. And also his choice of notes, his taste, his harmony. A sixth or a ninth or a seventh, the way he would lay these little things in there. Which he would do unconsciously too. Because those were things that were in his head harmonically and they came out on the cornet.
But what happened was this. After, to carry on in the Bix Beiderbecke vein, we copied all the numbers
off the recordings that they had made and (Gennett) records and we knew every number that they had recorded and knew it in the right key.
Now this was the Wolverines?

This was the Wolverines. With Bix Beiderbecke. And so I knew all the numbers off the records. Except the solos. I always played, we always had a rule with the Austin Highschool Gang, you play your own solo. So we knew all these numbers and I was playing a New Year's Eve job one night and Vic Moore the drummer who had been with the Wolverines and was not with them then, heard me. He said, man, You sound just like Bix you know. And I said, oh thanks, great.

So I got a wire a Western Union telegram, I'm going to Austin Highschool at the time, my second year, I'd almost finished my second year I think it was, starting the third year. And we had been playing a lot all around, professionally by then. I was seventeen years old. And the wire came from a guy by the name of Dick (Voynow) who was the leader and the piano player with the Wolverines.
How do you spell his last name?
Voynow, VOYNOW. And they were playing at the Cinderella Ballroom in New York City.

And the wire said, can you replace Bix Beiderbecke, $87.50 a week? Answer yes or no. (LAUGHTER). So I thought it was a gag because outside of King Oliver and the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, the Wolverines, those were the three top bands in the Country. Dixieland Jazz Band was one of the tops, but we liked King Oliver, Louis, by that time Louis had his own band, Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five. And Louis records were, oh man, they were too much. They used to knock us out.

So that was the Wolverines was the swingingest, the best. It was a white band if you want to call it that. I just figure everybody is a musician that is myself. A musician is a musician. So I get this wire and it said answer yes or no. So I did, I thought it was a gag. I thought somebody was kidding me. So I sent a wire which said 'yes' I can come. Wire transportation. So all the guys told me to do it.

By this time Benny Goodman was with us, had joined our group and Davey (Tottenham?). And so all the guys said send a wire anyway you know to see if it's on the level. So as I say, I got the wire back with a money order in it. And in those days I know it

was $32.50 for the train fare to New York City. So all the guys saw me off including Benny Goodman (Touph Tottenham, Frank Testemaker, Bud Freeman, my brother Dick and Jim Lanigan) and a lot of other people and family. And I left on a milk train from the South Street Station. (LAUGHTER). I had no idea, I just said I want a ticket to New York.
Were your parents still living then?
Oh yes.
Well they saw you at the start of your big career.
Yes. Well I asked them and they said well if you think it's the best thing to do. I said it couldn't be a greater honor in the whole world and that's the greatest thing.....
(inaudible).

That's it. So I went. I had not met Bix as yet. So I got there and Dick Voynow said rehearsal is two o'clock this afternoon. And I checked into this hotel there. I've forgotten the name of it right now, I'll think of it later. And we went over the rehearsal and he said, well what do you

play? And I told him, well anything you want, you guys have made records of. "Copenhagen you know, and "Need Some Petting" and so on and so forth." River Boat Shuffle." So we went ahead and we decided to play the numbers. And they were quite surprised that I knew all the numbers. You know, they were just flipping. Well do you know such and such? Do you know this tune and that tune? Sure, so I played. All the ensembles I had down. When it came time for my solo I played my own solo.

So that was it. So when the thing was over I said where's Bix, when do I get to meet Bix? He said, he's out there. And so I was cocky in those days but I didn't know he was out there. But I think if I'd known he was out there I would have been pretty nervous. (LAUGHTER). Believe me.
But I met Bix and he said, nice to meet you kid. And he said, I like you. He said, you sound like me but you don't copy me.
That was a high compliment.
Yes, it's the idea, you know. That's the story, you've got to be yourself. Play your own way. So Bix and I roomed together for a
couple of weeks there.
How old of a man was he then?
Well he was four years older than I was.
Oh. He was very young too?

Yes, but at that age, seventeen years old and twenty one you know, he used to call me kid. I had a bad horn and the horn was pretty tired and kind of beat up and so Dick Voynow said take the kid over and get him a new horn.

So Bix went over and picked me out a Conn Victor model which I paid for in installment plan you know. And we roomed together and he would show, they didn't have anything written down, because they couldn't read. So he had to show me these and in the day time we'd practice together and he would show me their arrangements, what notes I was to play and so forth on the tunes that were not on the records.
So we'd go on the job at night and play these numbers and I'd play the lead, that he had showed me and that he had taught me on these numbers.
I'd learn two or three numbers a day you know. And in that way over a period of two weeks why I got the whole repertoire. Know all the numbers. And then
he left and went with Jean Goldkette and his orchestra.
Oh that's what I was getting to.

Well that was his premise to begin with, he was waiting to go with Jean Goldkette and his orchestra with Jimmy Dorsey, Tommy Dorsey Joe Venuti, excuse me, and well he left to go with them. I stayed with the Wolverines and we went down to the Cinderalla Ballroom and we were there for about six or eight weeks I guess. We went to Florida and we were going to open up in a place on the Biscayne Bay, what was it, the Round House? I've forgotten.
In any case, you got there before Nixon huh? (LAUGHTER).
Yes. But what happened was the night we were supposed to open we came there and the Federal Agents closed on account of the eighteenth amendment. The Prohibition, it was during Prohibition.
See, this was 1924.
Yes, I was going to ask you about dates then. Now was that '24 when you came to
New York? Yes. I was seventeen years old.
Do you remember the month?

Oh yes, it was October. October, November, December we played the Cinderella Ballroom in New York and then went to Florida for this job down in Florida. Took a train down there but the night we were supposed to open ...
They raided it huh?
They raided it and we didn't have a job and no money.
To get back to New York.
(LAUGHTER).
No money.
This is the sad story in a musician's life. He's always stranded somewhere.
(LAUGHTER).

I tell you, I went three days without anything to eat. I was too proud to go and beg. And they were building a railroad across the Everglades and I bummed a ride, I hitched a ride out there. Somebody told me I could get a job. So when I got out there I went to the Foreman and he says,
kid, you don't want this job. This isn't for you. I said, oh why, I haven't, I haven't eaten in a couple of days. I'm hungry, I want to work. Make some money to eat.

So he said, look here, and he took me over and they were digging things up and all the snakes and stuff were coming up. And he said, you don't want this job. It's not so easy and you're a little too young. So he gave me a dime. He gave me a dime. So I took the dime and brought me an O'Henry bar and that's all I had to eat for three days. But anyway the next....
Well who was the leader of the Wolverines?
Dick Voynow.
Dick was the leader.
But they were all out of money.
Everybody was. broke.

But we had got a job, a one nighter down there with some guy by the name of Novak, some party M. And you could drink, people served you all the drinks you wanted, but I didn't want to drink, I wanted something to eat. (LAUGHTER). But the guy paid me after the job and I went to eat. I was

starving. And I got in this place and I ordered King Fish. Soup, King Fish and by the time I got to the King Fish I was eating so fast that I just couldn't hold it down. I had to run out and got sick. And the waitress said what's wrong? And I said, I've by then it was. haven't eaten in three or four days. So she said, well just eat some soup and you know.
All you had to do was look at that poor fish. (LAUGHTER).
That's right. So that's what happened on that.
You were saying that the something about the spirituals and the gospel music.

Well that's the greatest improvisation of jazz in the world, to me. That's basic, that's and I know when we heard, my brother and I heard these blind men down there on Lake and Polina Street, that that, we just flipped then.
And of course gospel and jazz are both urbanised forms of the original spiritual.
Well that's it, the spiritual. Didn't they used to be called the Holy Rollers or something like that or something?
Well that's just an aspect of store front, a store front variety.
But these are spirituals.
Well they tended to sing gospel music. We do make a distinction between the traditional spiritual and gospel music as such.
Oh, I see.

The original slaves and people on the plantations even after slavery who were singing spirituals were not singing what we now know as gospel music. And gospel music, of course both involved improvisation. But I would say that the spiritual involved improvisation with lyrics that's why some of them don't make sense. People just sang anything that came to their mind to keep the song going. The music and the rhythm going.
And that feeling, the feeling.
Yes, yes, yes, yes.
That's the most important thing. Well this is jazz.
But gospel music involved improvisation of the music itself too. Yes. Which is the clerical side of jazz.
As I say Helen, that was my brother and myself our first contact with what we call jazz now. Those eight blind men singing spirituals.

One of the reasons I said do you think, asked you whether that group was a negro group or not was that I have observed with the now jazz workshops that are being held in the various colleges around the Country. And Stan Kenton for example is perhaps the person most in demand for giving these jazz workshops. And the purpose of them is supposed to be to teach young people, particularly young white people, about jazz. And then again, however, sometimes you may have good taste and be a fine player, that you just cannot, the mood, you cannot make it. You just, something's wrong. The drummer's not playing right, the piano player hits a few bad chords or something like that. Or you yourself, I don't put all the blame on the accompanist or the rhythm section, or you yourself might just not,
might just not be in the groove you know and you just cannot get off the ground.
To me it's like a baseball player up there. Man, he gets up there and he's a real pro and a fine baseball player, but he can't hit that ball for sour apples. He can't even connect with it you know.
Of course the reverse side of that coin would be true too. That a soloist can make something even more exciting out of the original creation.
Well, that's true. That's true.

Oh I know sometimes, somebody comes along or maybe the mood is such that somebody in the band or in the group can galvanize the rest of the people into a real flow of inspired playing. It does work both ways.

It's like the article you were reading by George Frazier before, it's true, you give some, or someone gives you a spark. Well that's the empathy once again of musical conversation with musicians. They're talking with each other and to each other on their instruments. And sometimes someone goes off in a tangent and it doesn't flow well. It
just doesn't swing.

But you really have to try. Somebody once said something to me that really made an impression on me. And that was that no matter what's going on around you, try to play as if it was your last chance to really play. Play as if every solo was going to be your last. Give it that much attention and put that much into it.
I do that all the time. I try.
This is just close to what I said a while ago that when you get up there you really have only one chance.
You do.
That's it. Marian, you are opening January 2nd at which hotel? (LAUGHTER).

At the Carlisle and I'm quite excited about it, this is a new room for me. I've never played there. And actually, it's really you might say Bobby Short's room. He's played there for so many years. And it is partly due to Bobby that I'm going in there. He was kind enough to suggest me as somebody to play there for the two months that he's away and naturally, I'm looking forward to it very much.
Here's something very interesting. Bobby Short when I was in Chicago, that was in about
1930, oh gosh, 1930, oh what was it, 1935, '36?
Now don't date Bobby.
(LAUGHTER).

It doesn't make any difference because Bobby Short was a young kid, twelve years old. And I had a band that was playing at an hotel in Rockford, Illinois was it? One of those small towns out there, not Joliet...
He mentions that place in his book.
Yes. Well he was playing and he was a little act. He was a little act. He'd come up and play piano.
In a little white suit?

That's right. (LAUGHTER). Dressed up fit to kill and Bobby Short, he was about eleven, twelve years old. And he played the heck out of that piano at that time. And we accompanied him with the band you know, came in on his finales and so forth.
Listen, I'll have to go back to 'Black and White Baby' (LAUGHTER) and see what he says about you. (LAUGHTER).
Oh that's a very nice book. I enjoyed that a lot.
But how long will you be there?
Two months.
Oh yes, that's right.
And I just found out today, I was talking to George Wein (Weaver?).....
That's not really the question I meant to ask you, (LAUGHTER) I realised I repeated, I meant to ask you who was going to be there with you? But anyway, what did you find out today?

Well I'll tell you first the bass player that you met down in Annapolis, Rusty Gilder and a very good young drummer named Joe (Corcello?) who has worked with me. But what I found out today was that I'm going to be on the Newport Jazz Festival with my own group. And George said, let's not have a trio, why don't you augment the group and have some horn players which made me very excited because this really gives me a chance to do something that I want to do. And the second thing was that he's going to devote at least one or maybe two concerts to educational projects featuring the young musicians. Featuring this friend of mine, Clem DeRosa'. Or
rather some of the groups, some of the bands that he's put together, highschool bands and kids from the New York area will be playing at the 'Alice Tully' Hall.
Very good.
Yes. So that's going to be pretty exciting.
Yes, I should say so. Well I think I have to agree with you that this has been quite an afternoon Jimmy.
I loved it Helen.
And I'm just so happy that it's been my good fortune to do this work. (LAUGHTER).

To me it's always a pleasure to reminisce about great musical spirits that are no longer alive. But as I said before we fortunately have their music on records. But still somehow or other it doesn't make it to me, although some of them have made beautiful, marvellous records, inspiring and marvellous. But it's just a shame that you can't hear them all in person. Because they were so, I don't know, it's just different.
Well of course, I tend to think that all these people, their spirit is around somewhere.
Oh definitely.

And their spirit goes into the music that the people who are here are playing. So I feel in one form or another people like Louis, all the great musicians who have passed away, that their music is not only here on records, it's in people's memories and players who play still think of them.
It tends to exist as a creative force.
Right, a creative force, yes, that's what I wanted to say.

Well this may seem a little bit like the cart before the horse or the horse after the cart in this case. (LAUGHTER). But we started talking again after Marian came in and I think that we missed something that is tremendously important and that has to do with the fact that you spent a considerable amount of time in an orphanage.

That's right. My mother and father, let's see, I believe I was about six years old, five or six years old, it's after I started to play the violin, my mother and father were divorced. And they put us, my brother myself and my sister Ethel, the judge did, put us in a place called The Baptist Orphanage, in Maywood, Illinois.

And I guess I was there about altogether two and a half, three years, I'm not quite sure. I was rather young, but I know that we were in that orphanage. I was there a long time. My sister left first. My sister Ethel, went to live with one of my relatives. And then my brother left and went to live with my mother. And I was left there alone.

And I know I remember how I felt at that time. I really felt you know, left, alone. And I do think that this has affected me throughout my life somehow or other because instead of, I was very mad at everybody somehow or other. And I remember one of the matrons putting me, I'd done something, I'm not sure what it was, she put me in this attic and closed the door and she told me the tigers were going to get me and the animals and really scared the heck out of me.

I remember pounding on the door and crying and that's the last thing I remember because I evidently went to sleep I mean, I don't know. But I remember getting up, she woke me, came in and got me the next morning and came out and I was so mad and so, I got scared and felt, I just felt you know everybody's left me and everybody left, everybody left.

And the superintendent's son, Art McGilvery was his name, I remember. He said something to me or pushed me or something like that and I got mad and I started hitting him and knocked him through a glass door and he got out. And they really, there was the typical scene. It was snowing outside and they just made a big bag out of my clothes, clothing and wrapped it up in a bag, a paper bag and gave me three cents car fare to go to where my father was living in Oak Park. He had a room there someplace.
And I remember even this McGilvery guy, Art, helped me down to the station with my clothes.
And you were how old?

I was about seven, seven I guess or eight years old. Let's see, five, six, I was about eight I'd say. And he, the kid that I had the fight with and pushed through the door, helped carry my stuff down to the street car. And I got on the street car and I knew where my father lived. And it was that typical scene you know where it was snowing and everything else.
And you were the little match boy instead of the little match girl, huh, out in that show?
Yes, so I don't know, I never, I don't think I ever got over that. I always felt kind of alone, it made a sort of a loner out of me somehow or other. Inside. But it was quite a shocking experience.
Did you parents ever make it clear to you why you were left there?
Or why your brother was chosen?
Well my brother had already had rheumatic fever.
Oh that's right.

And he had a bad heart and so but no, they never did quite make it clear. Although I understood later on that they were getting a divorce and that was the reason that the judge had insisted that we go into the....
Well when you came out, when they put you out at that point, did you ever go back?
Oh no. No, I'm happy to say. Well my mother and father went back together again.
Oh did they?
Yes. We went back on the Lake Polina and my father set up a music school.
Well that's why I got the sense
of family then, yes, I see.

They went back together again and so on and so forth. And then we got in trouble, my brother and I for actually being bad boys. We had a little gang and everything. And we used to, well go out and steal and you know like that and we got put in jail.
Oh, how old were you then?
Twelve.
Oh God! (LAUGHTER).

Twelve, thirteen years old I guess. And we were put in jail and went to court and the judge insisted that my mother get us out of that neighborhood to a better environment. And that's when we went out to Austin. And I graduated grammar school at the John(Haye?) Grammar School in Austin and went on to Austin Highschool.

And fortunately, not long after I went to highschool I took up music and we got, wanted to play jazz. And I can say I just forgot about all those days and the music just encompassed me altogether. Jazz, music.
Yes, now I can understand, I mean at least there's more meaning for me to what Marian said that music really saved you from being a bad boy so to speak.

Well I agree because you just devote, you're so dedicated and it's something you want to, the compulsion is so great to want to play music that you have no time for anything else. And since I started to play why I've never been a bad boy.

Oh, that's beautiful. Just a bad man huh? (LAUGHTER). Now I'm very glad that we went back to this because I think it's all the more important for us to know that this was in your beginning as we talk about what has happened to you subsequently. And for you to have risen to the extremely high point that you did in the world of music and to have earned the honor of the best musicians we have in this Country the respect of these men, I think that it's a rather remarkable story. And as a matter of fact I like it better than rising from that to being president of a bank because they don't turn out to be very nice people. (LAUGHTER), afterwards. And I think you turned out to be very nice. (LAUGHTER).
Thank you Helen. I try really.
And now I think that we have come to the end of this rather, I think, rich conversation that's been hours long. This is Helen Armstead Johnston
again. And I have been talking with Jimmy and Marian McPartland as part of the project which Jazz Interactions is conducting for the National Endowment for the Arts in Washington.
Lois McCloud is the coordinator of the project and she works closely with Pastor John Gensel. the almost renowned in New York at least, Pastor to the jazz community, as he is known.
